\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates Information Extraction (IE) ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints.
A decidability analysis yields a two-layer architecture: a \emph{grammar layer} (context-free) compiles ontology constraints into grammars ensuring JSON validity and vocabulary membership; a \emph{semantic layer} (prefix-decidable with state) interprets type constraints at runtime via stateful token masking over a dynamic entity registry, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.
The two layers exhibit an empirical enabling dependency (Proposition~1): neither achieves full domain/range (DR) reduction alone.
% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
Composed with LoRA fine-tuning on three 8B-class models across two RE datasets (up to 96 relation types), \textsc{OntoCoDec} near-eliminates DR ($<$\,0.1\%) at R-F1 43--46\% ($\pm$0.8\,pp); residual cross-field violations (CF 0.2--1.3\% under fine-tuning) represent \emph{violation conversion}, resolved by beam search on SciERC (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Zero-shot evaluation serves as a diagnostic probe, revealing DR reduction of 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED across three models; constraint tightness ($\bar{\kappa}$) is a descriptive correlate of enforcement difficulty ($n{=}3$ schemas, $p{=}0.138$).
Preliminary 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}) and event extraction on WikiEvents (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}) confirm generalizability beyond the primary 8B evaluation.
\end{abstract}

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering improves precision but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}); at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it becomes impractical.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement; no method provides both semantic awareness and hard constraint enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with an \emph{empirical enabling dependency} between layers.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with preliminary 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 achieves near-complete DR elimination: DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% at R-F1 43--46\% ($\pm$0.8\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned; \S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); zero-shot evaluation reveals DR drops 42--99\% across models and datasets, with 76--99\% on SciERC, but total violations (DR+CF) decrease by $\sim$31\%, reflecting conversion that fine-tuning resolves (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).

We make a systematic engineering contribution with theoretical grounding:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework: we formalize a well-known intuition that cross-field type constraints require runtime state beyond context-free expressiveness (Proposition~1), yielding pair-based sequential enforcement at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas of varying restrictiveness with up to 96 relation types.
    \item A comprehensive evaluation across 3 IE datasets, 3 models (8B-class), and 2 tasks, with preliminary 70B validation: under fine-tuning, DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% at R-F1 43--46\% with CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\%; zero-shot ablation reveals an enabling dependency where on SciERC neither layer alone exceeds 24\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); event extraction on WikiEvents validates applicability beyond RE (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Downstream impact of violation removal.}
\label{app:downstream-impact}

A natural concern with schema-constrained decoding is whether enforcing ontological validity removes \emph{lucky violations}---predictions that happen to be correct (true positives) yet violate the schema.
To quantify this trade-off, we audit all true-positive relation triples produced by unconstrained fine-tuned models and check whether any of them carry a domain--range (DR) violation, i.e., an entity-type pair \mbox{$\langle h_\tau, t_\tau \rangle$} not sanctioned by the ontology for that relation.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llrrrl}
\toprule
\textbf{Dataset} & \textbf{Model} & \textbf{TP} & \textbf{Lucky} & \textbf{\%\,TP} & \textbf{R drop} \\
\midrule
SciERC & Qwen-LoRA  & 461  & 4 & 0.87\% & 0.41\,pp \\
SciERC & Llama-LoRA & 467  & 5 & 1.07\% & 0.51\,pp \\
DocRED & Qwen-LoRA  & 5746 & 1 & 0.02\% & 0.01\,pp \\
DocRED & Llama-LoRA & 6226 & 1 & 0.02\% & 0.01\,pp \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Lucky violations: true-positive triples that carry a domain--range violation. \textbf{Lucky} counts such triples; \textbf{R drop} is the recall decrease (in percentage points) if they were removed.}
\label{tab:lucky-violations}
\end{table}

Across all four configurations, lucky violations account for at most 1.07\% of true positives (5 out of 467 on SciERC with Llama-LoRA) and as few as 0.02\% on DocRED.
The corresponding recall drop is negligible---at most 0.51 percentage points---while the vast majority of violated triples that constraints remove are false positives.
For example, on DocRED with Qwen-LoRA, constraints eliminate 164 schema-violating predictions but only 1 of them is actually correct; the other 163 are errors that would pollute a downstream knowledge graph.

Inspecting the lucky violations qualitatively, they arise from borderline entity-type assignments rather than genuine schema gaps.
On SciERC, the recurring pattern involves \textsc{Metric}-typed entities (e.g., BLEU, NIST) appearing as heads of \texttt{Hyponym-of} relations, a pair absent from the training ontology because these metrics are rarely annotated as hyponyms.
On DocRED, the single lucky violation stems from an entity typed as \textsc{Misc} instead of \textsc{Org} (``Assassin's Creed Unity''), making its \texttt{developer} relation invalid under the schema despite being factually correct.

These findings confirm that schema-constrained decoding introduces a minimal recall cost while providing a substantial precision gain.
Retaining these few lucky violations would allow schema-invalid triples into the knowledge graph, undermining the structural guarantees that motivate constrained decoding in the first place.
The net effect is overwhelmingly positive: constraints act as a high-precision filter that removes far more erroneous triples than correct ones.

1	\section{Beam Search Compatibility}
2	\label{app:beam-search}
3	
4	OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is designed to be decoding-strategy agnostic.
5	The main experiments (\S\ref{sec:experiments}) use greedy decoding; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling} validates nucleus sampling.
6	Here we verify compatibility with beam search, completing coverage of the three standard decoding strategies.
7	
8	\paragraph{Implementation challenges.}
9	Two stateful components require adaptation for beam search.
10	(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
11	Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
12	(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
13	Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
14	Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.
15

\section{Beam Search Compatibility}
\label{app:beam-search}

OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is designed to be decoding-strategy agnostic.
The main experiments (\S\ref{sec:experiments}) use greedy decoding; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling} validates nucleus sampling.
Here we verify compatibility with beam search, completing coverage of the three standard decoding strategies.

\paragraph{Implementation challenges.}
Two stateful components require adaptation for beam search.
(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.

\paragraph{Results.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-search} compares beam search ($k{=}4$, \texttt{early\_stopping=True}) against greedy decoding under S1 constraints across six model-dataset combinations.

ET = entity type, RV = relation vocabulary, DR = domain/range, CF = cross-field consistency violation rates (\%); F1 $\times$ 100.}
\label{tab:beam-search}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%

  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.94} & 55.62 & 9.47 \\
\midrule

  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 13.40 & 1.27 & 27.46 & 3.67 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & 13.79 & \textbf{0.57} & 26.66 & 4.37 \\
\midrule

\paragraph{Discussion.}
For calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), beam search achieves DR=0\% across all four model-dataset combinations (both SciERC with 7 entity types, 551 documents, and DocRED with 96 relation types, 50 documents), regardless of schema complexity.
On SciERC, beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (0.93\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (0.08\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and substantially reduces CF (Qwen: 9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.53\%; Llama: 6.56\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
On DocRED (matched 50-document subsets), beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (8.69\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (1.58\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with CF reductions of 74\% and 86\% respectively.
Llama DocRED shows the largest R-F1 gain ($+$3.4\,pp), consistent with beam search recovering valid type assignments that greedy decoding missed due to constraint fallback.
The CF reduction is an indirect effect: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, avoiding the fallback-to-grammar path that produces cross-field inconsistencies under greedy decoding.

Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 25\% relative (28.4\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.
This contrast reveals that beam search resolves constraint-search failure (where greedy decoding encounters $G(t) \cap S(t) = \emptyset$ conflicts) but cannot overcome fundamental model calibration limitations in entity typing.

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering improves precision but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}); at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it becomes impractical.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement; no method provides both semantic awareness and hard constraint enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with an \emph{empirical enabling dependency} between layers.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with preliminary 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 achieves near-complete DR elimination: DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% at R-F1 43--46\% ($\pm$0.8\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types on both RE datasets under fine-tuning (1.54$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned; \S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); zero-shot evaluation reveals DR drops 42--99\% across models and datasets, with 76--99\% on SciERC, but total violations (DR+CF) decrease by $\sim$31\%, reflecting conversion that fine-tuning resolves (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).

We make a systematic engineering contribution with theoretical grounding:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework: we formalize a well-known intuition that cross-field type constraints require runtime state beyond context-free expressiveness (Proposition~1), yielding pair-based sequential enforcement at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas of varying restrictiveness with up to 96 relation types.
    \item A comprehensive evaluation across 3 IE datasets, 3 models (8B-class), and 2 tasks, with preliminary 70B validation: under fine-tuning, DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% at R-F1 43--46\% with CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\%; zero-shot ablation reveals an enabling dependency where on SciERC neither layer alone exceeds 24\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); event extraction on WikiEvents validates applicability beyond RE (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates Information Extraction (IE) ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints.
A decidability analysis yields a two-layer architecture: a \emph{grammar layer} (context-free) compiles ontology constraints into grammars ensuring JSON validity and vocabulary membership; a \emph{semantic layer} (prefix-decidable with state) interprets type constraints at runtime via stateful token masking over a dynamic entity registry, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.
The two layers exhibit an empirical enabling dependency (Proposition~1): neither achieves full domain/range (DR) reduction alone.
% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
Composed with LoRA fine-tuning on three 8B-class models across two RE datasets (up to 96 relation types), \textsc{OntoCoDec} near-eliminates DR ($<$\,0.1\%) at R-F1 43--46\% ($\pm$0.8\,pp); residual cross-field violations (CF 0.2--1.3\% under fine-tuning) represent \emph{violation conversion}, resolved by beam search on SciERC (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Zero-shot evaluation serves as a diagnostic probe, revealing DR reduction of 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED across three models; constraint tightness ($\bar{\kappa}$) is a descriptive correlate of enforcement difficulty ($n{=}3$ schemas, $p{=}0.138$).
Preliminary 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}) and event extraction on WikiEvents (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}) confirm generalizability beyond the primary 8B evaluation.
\end{abstract}

% Section 5 — SciERC Results (Draft)
% Data source: Phase 2 SciERC registry experiments
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_grammar_only,
%          phase2_scierc_semantic_only, phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_scierc_full_s2
% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

\subsection{Ablation and Composability with Fine-Tuning}
\label{sec:scierc-results}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} presents the five-way ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, zero-shot, 551 documents); only the active constraint layers differ across rows.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: SciERC five-way ablation
% ──────────────────────────────────────────

\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.6pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{6}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-7} \cmidrule(l){8-9}
\textbf{Mode}
  & DR\,$\downarrow$ & $\Delta$DR
  & RV\,$\downarrow$ & ET\,$\downarrow$ & CF & Tot.\,$\downarrow$
  & Rel.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
Unconstrained

  & 1.39  & 0.40
  & 0.08  & 15.45
  & 8.23  & 31.01 \\
Grammar
  & 14.84 & $\downarrow$3\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 0.08  & 14.92
  & 8.23  & 30.98 \\
GCD-equiv.$^\dagger$
  & 15.26 & $\downarrow$1\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 0.04  & 15.30
  & 8.75  & 30.91 \\
Semantic
  & 11.65 & $\downarrow$24\%
  & 1.51  & 0.40
  & 2.71  & 14.36
  & 8.15  & 31.01 \\
S1
  & \textbf{0.93} & $\downarrow$\textbf{94\%}
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 9.90  & \textbf{10.83}
  & \textbf{8.36} & 30.98 \\
S2
  & 0.97  & $\downarrow$94\%

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{Five-way ablation on SciERC (551 docs, Qwen3-8B, zero-shot).
$\Delta$DR: relative change vs.\ unconstrained.
Tot.\ = DR + CF (total type-violation burden).
Best per column in \textbf{bold} (CF excluded; Tot.\ included).
F1 $\times$100. Bootstrap: 10{,}000 iterations.
CF: same entity assigned conflicting types across triples.
S1 = single-pass (\S\ref{sec:strategies}), S2 = two-pass (\S\ref{sec:s2}).
Grammar-only represents the ceiling of grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}: vocabulary membership is enforced but cross-field semantic constraints are not.
$\dagger$GCD-equiv.: vLLM \texttt{guided\_json}~\cite{kwon2023vllm}, an independent grammar-constrained implementation confirming Grammar row equivalence (\S\ref{sec:constrained-baselines}).}
\label{tab:scierc-ablation}
\end{table}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic.}
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
S1 reduces DR from 15.37\% to 0.93\% ($\downarrow$94\%) with unchanged R-F1 ($p{=}0.58$), confirming the \emph{empirical enabling dependency}: grammar-only eliminates RV/ET but achieves only 3\% DR reduction; semantic-only reaches 24\%; their composition yields 94\% (Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}).
Total type-violation burden decreases from 15.45\% to 10.83\%, reflecting \emph{violation conversion} (CF 0.08\%\,$\to$\,9.90\%) that fine-tuning resolves (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
S2 achieves comparable DR but lower R-F1; we adopt S1.
Per-relation patterns and post-hoc comparison in Appendices~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape},~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning
%  exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,
%           w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,
%           w5_qwen_docred_lora_unconstrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval,
%           w5_llama_docred_lora_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
% exp_ids: bootstrap_ci_ft_composability.json, w5_lora_scierc_*, w8_*
Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}); adding S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% with no significant $\Delta$R-F1 after Bonferroni correction (min.\ $p{=}0.014$; 95\% CIs $\subseteq [-0.76, {+}0.22]$\,pp; removed triples are 97.6--100\% false positives).
A four-way ablation on fine-tuned models (Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}) reveals a qualitative shift: the grammar layer becomes a no-op (RV/ET already 0\%; DR change $<$0.2\,pp), making the semantic layer the sole effective DR defense (39--69\% independent reduction).
On SciERC, three relations with $\kappa \geq 0.36$ retain DR under fine-tuning alone (\textsc{Evaluate-for}: 13.1\%, \textsc{Part-of}: 5.8\%, \textsc{Compare}: 5.0\%); S1 eliminates all residual violations across all seven relations (Appendix~\ref{app:lora-per-relation}).
CF drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), concentrated in \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X type ambiguity (63.3\% of CF violations; Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}); beam ($k{=}4$) with LoRA eliminates all four violation types on SciERC (R-F1 43.60, 46.18; \S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll rrrr r@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Dataset} & \textbf{Mode}
  & \textbf{DR\,$\downarrow$} & \textbf{CF}
  & \textbf{R-F1\,$\uparrow$} & \textbf{E-F1\,$\uparrow$}
  & \textbf{$\Delta$DR} \\
\midrule
\multirow{4}{*}{Qwen3-8B}
  & \multirow{2}{*}{SciERC}
    & Unconstr.\ &  1.95 & 0    & 43.86 & 67.05 & --- \\
  & & S1    & \textbf{0} & 1.18 & 43.77 & 67.05 & $\downarrow$100\% \\
\cmidrule(l){2-8}
  & \multirow{2}{*}{DocRED}
    & Unconstr.\ &  0.56 & 0.08 & 40.89 & 82.35 & --- \\
  & & S1    & \textbf{0.00} & 0.22 & 40.79 & 81.87 & $\downarrow$100\% \\
\midrule
\multirow{4}{*}{\shortstack[l]{Llama\\3.1-8B}}
  & \multirow{2}{*}{SciERC}
    & Unconstr.\ &  1.11 & 0    & 45.45 & 67.76 & --- \\
  & & S1    &  0.09 & 0.46 & 45.47 & 67.76 & $\downarrow$92\% \\
\cmidrule(l){2-8}
  & \multirow{2}{*}{DocRED}
    & Unconstr.\ &  0.49 & 0.08 & 44.55 & 84.77 & --- \\
  & & S1    &  0.00 & 0.26 & 44.70 & 84.71 & $\downarrow$100\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{Fine-tuning composability: LoRA $\times$ unconstrained vs.\ S1 on SciERC (551 docs) and DocRED (998 dev docs).
F1\,$\times$100. No $\Delta$R-F1 is significant (Bonferroni-corrected; details in text); all DR reductions are ($p{<}0.001$).
E-F1 includes parse-failure documents (Qwen PF: 7--8\%; Llama PF: 2--3\%).}
\label{tab:composability}
\end{table}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (f) Downstream impact of DR elimination
%  exp_ids: task_e_lucky_violation_analysis
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Downstream impact.}
\label{sec:downstream-impact}
Among constraint-removed triples, only 0.49\% match gold labels (``lucky violations''; Appendix~\ref{app:lucky-violations}).
Error analysis of 514 false negatives (Qwen3-8B LoRA + S1) confirms only one (0.2\%) was blocked by constraints; the dominant error sources---relation type confusion (Part-of$\leftrightarrow$Used-for) and entity type polysemy---are schema-valid and beyond the reach of type constraints (Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Across all fine-tuned settings, only 36 residual DR violations remain, decomposing into entity type errors (39\%), schema coverage gaps (33\%), and relation/direction errors (28\%); the irreducible floor from coverage gaps is $\sim$3 violations (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).

\paragraph{Downstream impact of violation removal.}
\label{app:downstream-impact}

A natural concern with schema-constrained decoding is whether enforcing ontological validity removes \emph{lucky violations}---predictions that happen to be correct (true positives) yet violate the schema.
To quantify this trade-off, we audit all true-positive relation triples produced by unconstrained fine-tuned models and check whether any of them carry a domain--range (DR) violation, i.e., an entity-type pair \mbox{$\langle h_\tau, t_\tau \rangle$} not sanctioned by the ontology for that relation.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llrrrl}
\toprule
\textbf{Dataset} & \textbf{Model} & \textbf{TP} & \textbf{Lucky} & \textbf{\%\,TP} & \textbf{R drop} \\
\midrule
SciERC & Qwen-LoRA  & 461  & 4 & 0.87\% & 0.41\,pp \\
SciERC & Llama-LoRA & 467  & 5 & 1.07\% & 0.51\,pp \\
DocRED & Qwen-LoRA  & 5746 & 1 & 0.02\% & 0.01\,pp \\
DocRED & Llama-LoRA & 6226 & 1 & 0.02\% & 0.01\,pp \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Lucky violations: true-positive triples that carry a domain--range violation. \textbf{Lucky} counts such triples; \textbf{R drop} is the recall decrease (in percentage points) if they were removed.}
\label{tab:lucky-violations}
\end{table}

Across all four configurations, lucky violations account for at most 1.07\% of true positives (5 out of 467 on SciERC with Llama-LoRA) and as few as 0.02\% on DocRED.
The corresponding recall drop is negligible---at most 0.51 percentage points---while the vast majority of violated triples that constraints remove are false positives.
For example, on DocRED with Qwen-LoRA, constraints eliminate 164 schema-violating predictions but only 1 of them is actually correct; the other 163 are errors that would pollute a downstream knowledge graph.

Inspecting the lucky violations qualitatively, they arise from borderline entity-type assignments rather than genuine schema gaps.
On SciERC, the recurring pattern involves \textsc{Metric}-typed entities (e.g., BLEU, NIST) appearing as heads of \texttt{Hyponym-of} relations, a pair absent from the training ontology because these metrics are rarely annotated as hyponyms.
On DocRED, the single lucky violation stems from an entity typed as \textsc{Misc} instead of \textsc{Org} (``Assassin's Creed Unity''), making its \texttt{developer} relation invalid under the schema despite being factually correct.

These findings confirm that schema-constrained decoding introduces a minimal recall cost while providing a substantial precision gain.
Retaining these few lucky violations would allow schema-invalid triples into the knowledge graph, undermining the structural guarantees that motivate constrained decoding in the first place.
The net effect is overwhelmingly positive: constraints act as a high-precision filter that removes far more erroneous triples than correct ones.

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

OntoCoDec translates IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints.
LoRA + greedy S1 near-eliminates DR ($<$\,0.1\%, $<$0.5\% recall cost) with CF 0.2--1.3\%; beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violations on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency); zero-shot DR drops 42--99\% across three 8B-class models (\S\ref{sec:70b-results},~\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
The central insight is that IE type constraints exceed context-free expressiveness (Proposition~1): the semantic layer's entity registry provides random-access type lookups and forward masking~\cite{scholak2021picard,khorshidi2025odke}, bridging the gap grammar-only enforcement cannot address (3\% vs.\ 94\% DR reduction); this enabling dependency---scale-sensitive (\S\ref{sec:70b-results})---shows grammar-constrained decoding is necessary but insufficient for IE schema compliance.
Residual CF (0.2--1.3\%) arises from per-triple independent enforcement; global entity-level type consensus during decoding offers the most direct resolution (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic.}
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
S1 reduces DR from 15.37\% to 0.93\% ($\downarrow$94\%) with unchanged R-F1 ($p{=}0.58$), confirming the \emph{empirical enabling dependency}: grammar-only eliminates RV/ET but achieves only 3\% DR reduction; semantic-only reaches 24\%; their composition yields 94\% (Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}).
Total type-violation burden decreases from 15.45\% to 10.83\%, reflecting \emph{violation conversion} (CF 0.08\%\,$\to$\,9.90\%) that fine-tuning resolves (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
S2 achieves comparable DR but lower R-F1; we adopt S1.
Per-relation patterns and post-hoc comparison in Appendices~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape},~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
% exp_ids: bootstrap_ci_ft_composability.json, w5_lora_scierc_*, w8_*
Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}); adding S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% with no significant $\Delta$R-F1 after Bonferroni correction (min.\ $p{=}0.014$; 95\% CIs $\subseteq [-0.76, {+}0.22]$\,pp; removed triples are 97.6--100\% false positives; $\leq$1.1\% of true positives are affected across four fine-tuned configurations, with recall cost $\leq$0.51\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:downstream-impact}).
A four-way ablation on fine-tuned models (Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}) reveals a qualitative shift: the grammar layer becomes a no-op (RV/ET already 0\%; DR change $<$0.2\,pp), making the semantic layer the sole effective DR defense (39--69\% independent reduction).
On SciERC, three relations with $\kappa \geq 0.36$ retain DR under fine-tuning alone (\textsc{Evaluate-for}: 13.1\%, \textsc{Part-of}: 5.8\%, \textsc{Compare}: 5.0\%); S1 eliminates all residual violations across all seven relations (Appendix~\ref{app:lora-per-relation}).
CF drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), concentrated in \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X type ambiguity (63.3\% of CF violations; Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}); beam ($k{=}4$) with LoRA eliminates all four violation types on SciERC (R-F1 43.60, 46.18; \S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

\paragraph{Downstream impact.}
\label{sec:downstream-impact}
Among constraint-removed triples, only 0.49\% match gold labels (``lucky violations''; Appendix~\ref{app:lucky-violations}).
Error analysis of 514 false negatives (Qwen3-8B LoRA + S1) confirms only one (0.2\%) was blocked by constraints; the dominant error sources---relation type confusion (Part-of$\leftrightarrow$Used-for) and entity type polysemy---are schema-valid and beyond the reach of type constraints (Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Across all fine-tuned settings, only 36 residual DR violations remain, decomposing into entity type errors (39\%), schema coverage gaps (33\%), and relation/direction errors (28\%); the irreducible floor from coverage gaps is $\sim$3 violations (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering improves precision but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}); at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it becomes impractical.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement; no method provides both semantic awareness and hard constraint enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with an \emph{empirical enabling dependency} between layers.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with preliminary 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 achieves near-complete DR elimination: DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% at R-F1 41--46\% ($\pm$0.8\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types on both RE datasets under fine-tuning (1.54$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned; \S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); zero-shot evaluation reveals DR drops 42--99\% across models and datasets, with 76--99\% on SciERC, but total violations (DR+CF) decrease by $\sim$31\%, reflecting conversion that fine-tuning resolves (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).

We make a systematic engineering contribution with theoretical grounding:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework: we formalize a well-known intuition that cross-field type constraints require runtime state beyond context-free expressiveness (Proposition~1), yielding pair-based sequential enforcement at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas of varying restrictiveness with up to 96 relation types.
    \item A comprehensive evaluation across 3 IE datasets, 3 models (8B-class), and 2 tasks, with preliminary 70B validation: under fine-tuning, DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% at R-F1 43--46\% with CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\%; zero-shot ablation reveals an enabling dependency where on SciERC neither layer alone exceeds 24\% DR reduction (at 70B, semantic layer achieves 84\% independently; \S\ref{sec:70b-results}); event extraction on WikiEvents validates applicability beyond RE (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Preliminary 70B-class validation.}
\label{sec:70b-results}

-On Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (AWQ INT4), zero-shot S1 eliminates DR on both datasets: SciERC 6.41\%\,$\to$\,0\% (R-F1 11.24), DocRED 14.98\%\,$\to$\,0\% (R-F1 13.05); CF rises to 3.50--7.01\%, comparable to 8B zero-shot CF.

+On Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (AWQ INT4), zero-shot S1 eliminates DR on both datasets: SciERC 6.41\%\,$\to$\,0\% (R-F1 11.24), DocRED 14.98\%\,$\to$\,0\% (R-F1 13.05); CF rises to 0.04--3.50\%, comparable to 8B zero-shot CF.

\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates Information Extraction (IE) ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints.
A decidability analysis yields a two-layer architecture: a \emph{grammar layer} (context-free) compiles ontology constraints into grammars ensuring JSON validity and vocabulary membership; a \emph{semantic layer} (prefix-decidable with state) interprets type constraints at runtime via stateful token masking over a dynamic entity registry, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.
The two layers exhibit an empirical enabling dependency (Proposition~1, scale-sensitive; \S\ref{sec:70b-results}): neither achieves full DR reduction alone.
% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
Composed with LoRA fine-tuning on three 8B-class models across two RE datasets (up to 96 relation types), \textsc{OntoCoDec} near-eliminates DR ($<$\,0.1\%) at R-F1 43--46\% ($\pm$0.8\,pp); residual cross-field violations (CF 0.2--1.3\% under fine-tuning) represent \emph{violation conversion}; beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all four violation types under fine-tuning on both RE datasets (1.54$\times$ latency; \S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Zero-shot evaluation serves as a diagnostic probe, revealing DR reduction of 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED across three models; constraint tightness ($\bar{\kappa}$) is a descriptive correlate of enforcement difficulty ($n{=}3$ schemas, $p{=}0.138$).
Preliminary 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}) and event extraction on WikiEvents (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}) confirm generalizability beyond the primary 8B evaluation.
\end{abstract}
